name: Text to SQL Benchmarks
title: Text to SQL Benchmarks
answer: Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD score text to SQL systems by running the generated query and comparing its result with a known correct answer. These benchmarks usually measure execution accuracy, and sometimes exact match, across a set of questions and databases. They give a common yardstick for comparing models and pipelines. Enterprise schemas are larger and less tidy than the benchmarks, so real accuracy is usually lower.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Text to SQL benchmarks run on curated datasets that pair natural language questions with schemas and reference SQL. The harness executes generated SQL against a database instance, often SQLite for Spider and a mix of engines including PostgreSQL for BIRD. Evaluation can run on a single machine or in a container, with the database loaded from a dump or a script. The site itself is built from a PostgreSQL database, which is one of the engines these benchmarks commonly target.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with collecting questions and writing correct SQL for each one, then splitting the data into train, development, and test sets. Annotators check that the reference SQL runs and returns the expected result. During evaluation, a system generates SQL for each test question, the harness runs that SQL, and the result is compared with the reference result. Metrics such as execution accuracy and exact match are computed, and error analysis often looks at schema linking and join mistakes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because benchmark databases come from different sources, with different licenses and privacy expectations. Some datasets are public and permissively licensed, while others may include sensitive or proprietary schemas that cannot be redistributed. A risk is benchmark contamination, where test questions or schemas leak into training data and inflate scores. Another risk is overfitting to benchmark quirks, which can make a system look better than it is on a real enterprise schema.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward benchmarks that reflect enterprise conditions, with larger schemas, messy column names, and multi-turn questions. Newer evaluations look beyond execution accuracy to include efficiency, robustness to schema changes, and safety checks on generated SQL. There is growing interest in dynamic benchmarks that change over time to resist contamination. The site tracks 263 Model Context Protocol servers for SQL databases and warehouses, a sign that SQL access is becoming a common building block. This tooling may shape how text to SQL systems are tested and deployed.
